title: Death at a Funeral
full_review:
The delightful animated credits and music that open this black comedy bode well. And, indeed, "Death at a Funeral" (MGM/Sidney Kimmel) proves to be in the best tradition of British farces even though directed by American -- if English-born -- comedy veteran Frank Oz.

Chaos runs rampant as family members gather for a patriarchal funeral and everything goes wildly wrong. There's arrogant, famous novelist son Robert (Rupert Graves); insecure second son and aspiring writer Daniel (Matthew MacFadyen), trying desperately to make the funeral come off without a hitch (and hoping he'll deliver an excellent eulogy); the latter's exasperated wife, Jane (Keeley Hawes); and cousin Martha (Daisy Donovan) and her strait-laced fiance, Simon (Alan Tudyk).

Things go seriously awry when a mysterious guest, Peter (Peter Dinklage), shows up and -- scandalous photos in hand -- threatens a damaging revelation, prompting the sons to do everything in their power to silence him. Simon, meanwhile, has inadvertently ingested a hallucinatory drug and, to the family's bewilderment, begins to act in a highly peculiar fashion. This eventually includes taking off his clothes and tottering precariously on the roof. (There's some benign side and rear nudity during these shenanigans.)

Oz whips up a skillfully farcical frenzy, and the cast is game, with Tudyk delivering a truly outstanding comic performance. Those who saw MacFadyen as Darcy in the recent "Pride and Prejudice" film will be surprised at his versatility here, playing such a pallid character. And good sport Dinklage allows his diminutive stature to factor significantly in all the mayhem.

This is an ensemble comedy, however, and the cast is uniformly accomplished, including Peter Vaughn as cranky (and incontinent) Uncle Alfie; Andy Nyman as Daniel's hypochondriac friend, Howard; Ewan Bremner as Justin, who's determined to rekindle his brief affair with Martha; Jane Asher as widow Sandra; and Peter Egan as Martha's critical dad, Victor.

But recommendation must be tempered by the overload of expletives in Dean Craig's otherwise quirky and funny script; they start well before the manic action that might arguably (from a purely dramatic standpoint) justify their use later on.

The overall irreverence (in a nonreligious sense) may offend some viewers, though in the tradition of classic farce, everything gets sorted out by the end with a validation of family and, despite all the havoc, reconciliation and redemption come into play, with the experience being particularly transformative for the hapless Daniel.

The film contains gratuitous and pervasive profanity, rough and crude language, rear male nudity, drug use, homosexual blackmail theme, innuendo and scatological humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
